Passage 1: Lanterns Over the Ping — Ecology and Evolution of Yi Peng & Loy Krathong

Questions 26–30

A Every November, on the full moon of the twelfth lunar month, communities across northern Thailand gather along the Ping River to celebrate two intertwined traditions: Loy Krathong and Yi Peng. While Loy Krathong centers on releasing small buoyant vessels—traditionally fashioned from banana-tree trunks and folded banana leaves—onto rivers and canals, Yi Peng is distinguished by launching thousands of heated paper lanterns, known locally as khom loi, into the night sky. Symbolically, both rituals invite participants to let go of past misfortune and express gratitude to the water goddess, Phra Mae Khongkha.

B Over the past two decades, however, the rapid expansion of international tourism has transformed what was once an intimate neighborhood observance into a large-scale visual spectacle. Municipal authorities in Chiang Mai now confront a delicate balancing act: preserving cultural heritage while safeguarding urban infrastructure and aviation corridors. Because drifting lanterns pose a documented hazard to aircraft engines and power lines, flight schedules at Chiang Mai International Airport are routinely modified during peak release windows.

C Parallel environmental concerns have reshaped the design of krathongs themselves. During the 1990s, inexpensive styrofoam bases briefly replaced organic materials, leaving municipalities to clear tons of non-biodegradable debris the following morning. Today, civic campaigns promote bread-dough floats, ice krathongs, and natural banana-stalk models pinned with wooden toothpicks rather than metal staples. Yet freshwater ecologists caution that even bread krathongs, when deposited in excessive concentrations inside stagnant ponds, can deplete dissolved oxygen as they decompose.

D Consequently, several Thai universities and city districts have introduced "digital krathong" projections onto riverbanks and encouraged families to share a single biodegradable vessel instead of floating one per person. Such adaptations illustrate that enduring festivals survive not through rigid immobility, but through pragmatic ecological stewardship.

Passage 2: Water, Renewal, and Urban Density — Songkran in Comparative Perspective

Questions 31–35

A Held annually from April 13 to 15, Thailand's Songkran festival marks the traditional solar New Year at the height of the dry season. Historically, the ritual of pouring jasmine-scented water over the hands of elders—called rod nam dam hua—served as a quiet gesture of filial respect and spiritual purification. In contemporary metropolitan centers such as Bangkok and Chiang Mai, however, this gentle custom coexists with boisterous street-level water fights that attract millions of domestic and overseas visitors.

B Anthropologists frequently compare Songkran with other sensory-intensive celebrations worldwide, including India's Holi and Spain's La Tomatina. Although all three festivals temporarily suspend everyday social hierarchies through playful physical immersion, they diverge sharply in climate timing, resource footprint, and crowd-management strategy. Whereas Holi celebrates the transition from winter to spring with dry mineral and herbal pigments, Songkran's reliance on municipal water supplies raises urgent sustainability questions during severe El Niño droughts.

C To reconcile celebratory energy with civic safety, urban planners have evaluated traffic-free pedestrian zones and water-conservation nozzles. Compared with unrestricted roadside splashing, designated pedestrian corridors reduce road-accident rates considerably while allowing emergency vehicles unobstructed access along parallel arteries. At the same time, cultural educators emphasize that the festival's most resilient asset is its multigenerational core: families still begin the holiday with morning merit-making at local temples long before the afternoon street crowds assemble.
